title: __init__ and Attributes: Give Every Object Its Own Data From the Start
excerpt: Stop forgetting to set object data: __init__ runs when an object is created and gives every object its own attributes.

headings.text: __init__ Runs When You Create an Object

html:
Creating an empty object and then attaching its data one attribute at a time is fragile. Forget one line and the object is missing something that the rest of your code assumes is there. You want every new object to be set up completely the moment it is created.

__init__ is a special method that Python runs automatically whenever you create an object, so it is the place to give the object its starting data. This lesson shows how it works, what self is doing, and the difference between data that belongs to each object and data shared by the whole class.

Three terms first: a class is a blueprint, an object is one thing built from it, and an attribute is a piece of data stored on an object. The word pass simply means "an empty body, nothing to add".

The Fragile Way

Here is what happens when nobody sets an object's data:

class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
print(rex.name)
AttributeError: 'Dog' object has no attribute 'name'

The object exists, but nobody gave it a name, so reading the name fails with an AttributeError: Python is saying the object has no value stored under that name. With many objects and many attributes, remembering to set everything every time is a recipe for bugs.

__init__ Runs When You Create an Object

The name has two underscores before and after it. Define it inside the class, and Python calls it for you every time you write Dog(...), passing along the arguments you gave:

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        print("creating", name)
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
fido = Dog("Fido", 5)

print(rex.name, rex.age)
print(fido.name, fido.age)
creating Rex
creating Fido
Rex 3
Fido 5

The two creating lines show that __init__ ran by itself, once per object. Who passes the first parameter, self? Python does. It hands the brand-new object to __init__ as self, and the arguments you wrote fill the remaining parameters.

What self.name = name Means

The line self.name = name looks odd the first time. Why write the same name twice? Because they are two different things. The part on the left, self.name, is an attribute stored on the object. The part on the right, name, is the parameter that was passed in. Together they say "store this value on the object". If you leave out self., you only create an ordinary local variable (a name that exists only inside this one method call) that disappears when the method ends:

class Cat:
    def __init__(self, name):
        name = name

tom = Cat("Tom")
print(tom.name)
AttributeError: 'Cat' object has no attribute 'name'

This is one of the most common beginner mistakes. The attribute was never created, because nothing was ever stored on self.

Default Values

__init__ is an ordinary function in every other way, so its parameters can have defaults:

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age=1):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

puppy = Dog("Bolt")
print(puppy.name, puppy.age)
Bolt 1

Instance Attributes and Class Attributes

Everything set with self. belongs to one object (an instance of the class), so these are called instance attributes. You can also put a value directly in the class body, where it is shared by every object, called a class attribute:

class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

rex = Dog("Rex")
fido = Dog("Fido")

print(Dog.species, rex.species, fido.species)

rex.species = "wolf"
print(rex.species, fido.species, Dog.species)

Dog.species = "dog"
print(fido.species, rex.species)
Canis familiaris Canis familiaris Canis familiaris
wolf Canis familiaris Canis familiaris
dog wolf

Setting rex.species gave only Rex his own value, which takes priority over the shared one for him alone. Why did Fido change but Rex did not? Changing Dog.species changed it for every object without its own value, so Fido saw the new value, while Rex kept his own.

The Shared List Trap

Class attributes are fine for constants (values that never change). They become dangerous when the value is something you can change, such as a list (the method append adds an item to its end), because every object shares that one list:

class Dog:
    tricks = []

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

rex = Dog("Rex")
fido = Dog("Fido")

rex.tricks.append("sit")
print(fido.tricks)
['sit']

Rex learned a trick, and suddenly Fido knows it too. The fix is to create the list inside __init__, so every object gets its own:

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.tricks = []

rex = Dog("Rex")
fido = Dog("Fido")

rex.tricks.append("sit")
print(rex.tricks)
print(fido.tricks)
['sit']
[]

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonInitAttributes.ipynb.

Summary

  • __init__ runs automatically when an object is created, and sets up its starting data.
  • Python passes the new object as self; your arguments fill the other parameters.
  • self.name = name stores the value on the object; without self. it is only a local variable.
  • Parameters of __init__ can have defaults like any other function.
  • A class attribute is shared by all objects; an instance attribute belongs to one object.
  • Never put a list or dictionary in a class attribute if each object needs its own; create it in __init__.
